paragraphs.text:
Chronological Instruction for the Monastery of Stoudios, by our father among the saints Theodore the Studite. (The Studite wrote many catecheses, but this one is called the Chronological Catechesis.)

1. Brothers and Fathers, to you who wish to live rightly and in a way pleasing to God, I wish to show as clearly as I can how we must keep the yearly cycle of the seasons, both for the piety of the faithful and for the refutation of the heretics. Salt is good and light is good. But anyone outside these is blind and does not know where he is going, as our Lord said. Whoever sets out to build a house of orthodoxy must lay an unshakable foundation on the canons handed down by the divine apostles and the God-bearing Fathers. Above all, let us see what the sacred word has said. Long ago the Lord said to Moses, who revealed sacred things: "Keep three seasons of the year for me, a holy fast, from the least of you to the greatest. At the feast of unleavened bread in the first month, humble your souls for seven days and eat the bread of affliction. Then seven weeks shall be counted for you, fifty full days, and you shall call it a holy day of assembly, an acceptable fast. And on the tenth [?], in the middle of the year, you shall have a holy feast, the Feast of Tabernacles. You shall humble your souls before your God, and every soul that is not humbled shall be destroyed from among you." It seems that this is why we too keep three fasts, which those feasts foreshadowed. What, then, brothers, does "Keep three seasons of the year for me, a holy fast, from the least of you to the greatest" mean for us? I think it is a pure type of the one and only Godhead, which we who worship the truth see and worship in three persons. So the divine disciples of the only-begotten Son of God laid down three fasts for us as a type of the Trinity, the source of life. Again, let two days

out of the seven be kept pure for you, that is, Wednesday and Friday. What does "Let two days out of the seven be kept pure" mean? I think it means this: in the recurring cycle of the seven-day wheel, let two be kept pure, namely the divinity and the humanity of the one Son, supremely united, who is Son of God and of the holy Mother. Another view is that the weekly cycle also marks the type of the Trinity by three days, just as the faithful clearly honor the pure type of the Trinity over the year.

2. The first forty-day fast. The first fast is the one for the feast of Christ's Nativity. It may be taken as a type of the Father, as he knows who was himself well pleased with the conception and birth of the Son. That is why forty days have been laid down for it, like the fast of Moses and of Elijah.

3. The second fast. The second fast after it, also called Great Lent, may be a type of the Only-begotten. He showed it clearly himself by keeping it for three years after he came up from baptism. If you ask how this is clear, listen to me, hearer, and look carefully. The Lord evidently received baptism at thirty years of age and underwent death three years later. So, as we have learned from those with the most exact knowledge, he set the example of this fast three times, once each year.

4. The third fast. The third fast after it, which some call the fast of the apostles, may be a type of the life-giving Spirit, who also taught the apostles everything that the Father and the Son had revealed. The three have one name, the Godhead, but it is known and worshiped in three hypostases.

5. But let us go on. The discourse will now come to the subject itself. We will set out each thing in its own season, by days and by weeks, and give the reason for each rule. Let Wednesday and Friday always be kept entirely pure for fasting, without cheese, fish or oil, as the divine apostles and the God-bearing Fathers after them laid down. But for the Nativity of the all-immaculate Theotokos, her Entry into the Temple, the feast called the Meeting, the Annunciation and her divine Translation, we relax the fast to allow oil and fish if these feasts fall on the days named, Wednesday and Friday. We do the same for the Nativity of the Forerunner and for the feast of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. But for the feasts of the holy martyrs and holy hierarchs we do not relax the fast to allow fish if they fall on Wednesday or Friday.

6. To the glory and praise of the wood of the Cross, some monks keep fourteen days of fasting, others twelve and others four. But the whole people of Christ all keep pure the day of the Exaltation itself, that is, the fourteenth of September. In the fast of Christ's Nativity, let three days of the week be kept without fish and oil, namely Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and let one

fast devoutly. Let the fast of the holy apostles and the holy fast of the Mother of God be kept in the same way. On the eve of Christ's Nativity we keep fasting, and we keep the day pure of fish and oil, except when it falls on a Saturday or Sunday. Then we eat them. We do the same on the eves of Christ's other feasts. But on the following day we relax the fast, whatever day it falls on, as we said above, to the glory of the Father who was well pleased and of the Son who was born. We relax the fast on that day and on six more, so that we may not look gloomy at the birth of the one who refashioned us, as the ungrateful Jews did.

7. We likewise pass the eve of the Lights fasting, abstaining from oil, fish and other foods for the whole day. But on the day of the Theophany itself, whatever day it falls on, we relax the fast to allow everything. We do this in thanks and glory to the one who was baptized, for the holy beginning of this grace, and as a public celebration of the drowning of the slayer of mortals. Our joy at this is like the following. Suppose a man has received a gift of wealth from a king. He keeps it and enjoys the good things he has received. After a while, an enemy, an arrogant rebel, springs up from somewhere, robs him of this wealth and treats him violently as well. The king learns of it, comes, punishes that rebel without mercy and restores the stolen wealth to its owner. He even bestows on him, beyond what he had before, a royal token that strikes fear into his adversaries. In just this way our Lord dealt with the rebel enemy and gave us the grace of regeneration, greater than the former gift. In our rebirth through water and the Spirit, this cleansing is twofold for us: the body is washed by the water, and the spirit is renewed by the Spirit. How can we fail to rejoice and dance for our salvation? I believe that whoever does not rejoice on this day of holy baptism does not regard this grace as saving. Instead he shows himself gloomy, and his attitude toward the saving [?] is godless and wicked.

On the Week of Proclamation.

8. Likewise we relax the Week of Proclamation, in which the holy Gospel of the tax collector and the Pharisee is read, to allow every kind of food, as we received from the holy Fathers before us. This is not for some reason of orthodoxy, as with the weeks of the Nativity and the holy Theophany [?] kept fasting [?]

[?] is relaxed. It is done to undo the godless doctrine of the utterly profane Peter, bishop of the Armenians, whom tradition calls Lycopetrus, "Wolf-Peter." That thrice-accursed man laid down a rule for his followers that they should keep this whole week pure by fasting, all because of some stupid and utterly loathsome wolf. But we, the Lord's people, relax the whole week to overturn them and their godless and senseless doctrine. Gregory, great in theology, also bears witness somewhere to their inhumanity, saying, "I find the Armenian race not simple, but rather hidden and treacherous like a sunken reef." Here he is mocking the treachery of their faith. Likewise we relax the Week of Cheese-fare after the ninth hour to allow cheese and eggs, so as to overturn the impious religion of the Jacobites and Tetradites. I believe the holy Fathers forbade eating meat in this cheese-eating week to recall the monastic order, or as a type of the new and pure way of life.

9. During holy and Great Lent we eat once a day, at the ninth hour. We eat dry food, or pulses without oil, and no wine, except on Saturday and Sunday. We also eat all kinds of shellfish, [?] and salted fish without hesitation. But we do not eat fish at all during this holy fast, except on the Saturday and on Palm Sunday. This is to the glory of the one who came out of his fast and shared a meal after the raising of Lazarus. Or else it is plainly because this too is one of Christ's divine feasts. We keep Holy and Great Week entirely fasting, if possible, with neither oil nor wine. The exception is the vigil of the holy Passion, when one may drink something as needed because of the toil. Likewise we keep fasting until evening on Great Saturday, on that Saturday alone and on no other in the whole year. We also relax the fast for the whole Week of Renewal, to the glory of the Son of God who gave us life. If anyone does not eat during this week without hesitation, but keeps a gloomy face in the Jewish manner, let him fall under the anathema of the holy Fathers.

10. From the Monday of Thomas Week we begin to commemorate our departed brothers, and on Wednesday and Friday we abstain from meat and cheese. Some of the holy Fathers before us decided to relax the fast on the Wednesday of Mid-Pentecost, because it is a feast of the Lord, and for this reason [?]

[?]. Christ is called the cornerstone, and he is the cornerstone, joining the two covenants together into one. In the same way, this day joins the Resurrection to the coming of the Spirit. This feast of the Only-begotten appears joyful, since he himself is glorified and worshiped as the mediator between Godhead and manhood. That is why those before us celebrated it without hesitation and ate everything. But now let anyone who can accept this accept it on this day, if possible. We also relax the week of the Holy Spirit to allow everything, because of the coming of the Spirit. For just as we must rejoice at the Son's birth and at his life-giving resurrection, we must also rejoice at the Spirit's descent.

11. Let everyone know that the three weeks of the Nativity, the Resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit may be taken by us as a type of the Trinity, the source of life, in three hypostases. The two after them, the weeks of Proclamation and of Cheese-fare, are relaxed because of the heresies mentioned above, so that we may not seem to follow the utterly unholy teachings of those people. The fast also called the fast of the apostles we keep like the fast of Christ's Nativity, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. If the day of the apostles, the two among the twelve, falls on Wednesday or Friday, we do not relax the fast to allow meat and cheese, but only fish and oil. We keep the fast of the Theotokos in the same way. On the day of the Transfiguration itself we relax the fast to allow fish and oil. It ought to be relaxed differently, but the fast prevents it. If the day of the holy Dormition of the all-blameless Mother of God falls on Wednesday or Friday, we do not relax the fast to allow meat or cheese. This is because of the great and awesome wonder of that extraordinary sleep. As we have found in the divine writings of Clement of Rome, the Savior's divine apostles waited at the tomb for three full days at that time, until a divine angel revealed the whole mystery to them. Likewise, if the Beheading of the divine Forerunner falls on Wednesday or Friday, we do not relax the fast, because this day too recalls an unholy murder and death.

12. Here ends my treatise, brothers, drawn from what I read in the divine writings and most lawful canons of the apostolic and holy Fathers. We have firmly built the house of orthodoxy that this discourse set out to build from the beginning. I am therefore firmly and steadfastly confident in the one God worshiped in Trinity that, for orthodoxy, [?] writes thus: Relax the fast to allow everything on the Wednesday of Mid-Pentecost, as our God-bearing Father Theodore of Stoudios handed down to us [?] (cf. Matthew 19:12): Let anyone who can accept this accept it.
